q: A fitness app wants to collect a user’s location to show nearby classes. What should it do before collecting location data?
a: Give a clear, standalone notice describing the location data and the specific purpose, then obtain valid consent unless a lawful exception applies.
why: Consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, signified by clear affirmative action. The notice must describe the personal data and purpose.
law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 6(1)–(2); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 3
bad: Collect it silently because location improves the service.
Bundle it into broad terms and make consent mandatory for unrelated features.
Ask for permission only after the data has been collected.

q: A customer withdraws consent for personalized offers but still wants to use the basic service. What is the best response?
a: Stop processing for personalized offers and make withdrawal as easy as giving consent; continue any separately justified core processing.
why: A Data Principal may withdraw consent at any time, with ease comparable to giving it. The Act does not require withdrawal from one purpose to end unrelated processing that has its own lawful basis.
law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 6(4)–(6); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 3(c)
bad: Keep using the data because the customer accepted terms originally.
Delete the entire account immediately, even if the person wants to keep using it.
Require a signed paper letter when consent was given with one tap.

q: A shopping service collected phone numbers to send delivery updates. Marketing now wants to use the same list for promotions. What should happen?
a: Do not repurpose the numbers automatically; provide an appropriate notice and obtain consent for the new purpose, unless a specific lawful use applies.
why: Personal data may be processed for a lawful purpose for which consent was given or for certain legitimate uses set out in the Act. A delivery notice does not itself authorize promotional use.
bad: Use the list because marketing benefits the company.
Assume delivery consent covers all future communications.
Share the list with an ad partner and let it decide what is allowed.

q: A scholarship portal needs to verify eligibility. Its form asks every applicant for their full contact list and unrelated browsing history. What is the compliant design choice?
a: Collect only personal data needed for the stated eligibility and service purposes, and remove unrelated fields.
why: The Act requires processing for a lawful purpose and its consent framework requires a specific purpose. Data collection should match that purpose; unrelated data is not justified by convenience.
law: DPDP Act, 2023, ss. 4 and 6(1); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 3
bad: Collect everything now in case another department needs it later.
Keep the fields but label them optional while making submission impossible without them.
Collect unrelated data because users can ask for deletion later.

q: A learning game is designed for children under 18 and wants to use behavioral ads. What should the operator do?
a: Obtain verifiable consent from a parent or lawful guardian and do not undertake tracking, behavioral monitoring or targeted advertising directed at children, subject to applicable exemptions.
why: The Act defines a child as a person under 18. Before processing a child’s personal data, verifiable parental consent is required; tracking, behavioral monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children are restricted, subject to prescribed exceptions.
bad: Treat the child’s click as sufficient adult consent.
Run behavioral ads if the game is free.
Collect first and ask a parent only if an issue arises.

q: A company discovers that an employee exported customer records to an unsecured personal drive. What should the company prioritize?
a: Contain the exposure, investigate, restore appropriate safeguards, and follow applicable breach notification requirements.
why: Data Fiduciaries must take reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breaches. If a breach occurs, they must notify the Board and affected Data Principals in the prescribed manner.
law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 8(5)–(6); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 7
bad: Wait to see whether anyone complains before securing the files.
Delete the audit logs so the incident cannot be misunderstood.
Notify only the employee who exported the data.

q: A cloud provider reports that personal data held for your company was exposed. Who remains responsible for ensuring required breach notices are made?
a: The Data Fiduciary remains responsible for complying with the Act, including notifying the Board and affected Data Principals as prescribed.
why: A Data Fiduciary remains responsible for processing undertaken by it or on its behalf, including by a Data Processor. Section 8(6) requires notice of a personal data breach to the Board and each affected Data Principal.
bad: The cloud vendor alone, because it hosted the information.
The affected individuals, because they should monitor their accounts.
No one, if the provider promises to fix its security.

q: A startup hires a vendor to send appointment reminders using customer names and phone numbers. What should the startup do?
a: Use a valid contract with the processor and ensure appropriate safeguards and compliance for processing done on its behalf.
why: A Data Fiduciary may engage a Data Processor under a valid contract, but remains responsible for compliance with the Act in respect of processing undertaken by it or on its behalf.
bad: Send the data without a contract because the vendor is reputable.
Assume the vendor becomes the only responsible party.
Allow the vendor to use the numbers for its own unrelated advertising.

q: An event ticketing company has finished handling a ticket purchase and has no legal or operational reason to keep the attendee’s extra profile data. What next?
a: Erase the data when its purpose is no longer served, unless retention is required by law, and cause processors to erase it too.
why: The Data Fiduciary must erase personal data when consent is withdrawn or the specified purpose is no longer served, unless retention is required by law. Check applicable minimum retention rules before erasing processing records.
law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 8(7); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 8(3)
bad: Keep all profiles forever for possible future analytics.
Keep copies with processors after deleting the main database.
Erase only when the individual files a formal complaint.

q: A user asks a service for a summary of the personal data being processed and the processing activities. What should the service do?
a: Provide the information the user is entitled to under the Act, following a reasonable identity and request-handling process.
why: A Data Principal has a right to obtain a summary of personal data being processed and the processing activities, subject to the Act and prescribed manner.
bad: Reject the request because the data belongs to the company.
Demand a court order for every rights request.
Send another person’s data too to prove the system is complete.

q: A user points out that their profile has an incorrect spelling of their name. What is the proper response?
a: Provide a way to request correction and take appropriate steps to correct inaccurate personal data.
why: The Act grants the Data Principal a right to correction, completion and updating of personal data, in accordance with applicable requirements.
bad: Refuse because the user entered the name initially.
Correct it only if the user withdraws all consent.
Leave it wrong but mark the profile as disputed.

q: A customer says the app ignored a deletion request and wants to raise a privacy complaint. What should the company have in place?
a: An accessible grievance redressal mechanism and a timely response process, with the option to approach the Board after exhausting it.
why: Data Fiduciaries must establish an effective mechanism to redress grievances. Data Principals must exhaust the opportunity to raise a grievance with the Data Fiduciary or Consent Manager before approaching the Board.
bad: Hide the contact details until the customer closes the account.
Require the customer to post publicly on social media.
Tell the customer only a court can handle privacy complaints.

q: A lender uses profile data to make a decision that affects a customer. It finds contradictory records. What should it do?
a: Take reasonable steps to ensure the data is complete, accurate and consistent before using it for a decision affecting the person.
why: Where personal data is likely to be used to make a decision affecting a Data Principal or disclosed to another Data Fiduciary, the Data Fiduciary must ensure completeness, accuracy and consistency.
bad: Use whichever record gives the fastest result.
Ignore the conflict because the data came from a vendor.
Publish both records and ask the customer to choose publicly.

q: A user wants to exercise rights or report a concern. What information should the Data Fiduciary make available?
a: Business contact information for a person able to answer questions about processing and rights requests.
why: The Act requires a Data Fiduciary to publish the business contact information of its Data Protection Officer, if applicable, or another person able to answer questions on its behalf.
bad: Only the name of the cloud provider.
A private employee directory with no relevant contact.
No contact information unless a breach occurs.

q: Your analytics processor proposes adding a new subcontractor that will access identifiable user events. What should you do first?
a: Assess the proposed processing, ensure it is covered by the contract and safeguards, and authorize access only when it serves the stated purpose.
why: The Data Fiduciary remains responsible for processing on its behalf and must use reasonable security safeguards. Vendor access should be governed by a valid contract and the purpose disclosed to the Data Principal.
bad: Allow access because the processor chose the vendor.
Permit unrestricted reuse if the subcontractor signs an NDA.
Treat hashed or pseudonymous data as automatically outside all obligations.

q: A regulator asks how a user consented to a specific data use. What is a sound operational practice?
a: Keep records that can demonstrate the notice presented and the affirmative consent action for that purpose.
why: The Data Fiduciary bears the burden of proving that notice was given and consent was obtained in accordance with the Act when consent is relied upon.
bad: Rely only on a general statement that users accepted the terms.
Recreate a consent record after the request arrives.
Use one consent record for purposes added years later.

q: A public authority receives a request to process personal data for a function imposed by law. What is the right first question?
a: Check whether the specific processing falls within a lawful ground, such as a use permitted under section 7, and observe applicable requirements.
why: The Act permits processing for certain legitimate uses, including specified functions under law, subject to statutory conditions. A public authority should identify the applicable ground rather than assume every government use is automatically permitted.
bad: Assume government status removes every privacy obligation.
Collect any data that might be useful someday.
Treat the request itself as blanket consent.

q: A service stores data with a cloud provider outside India. What does the DPDP Act say as a baseline?
a: Cross-border transfer is permitted unless the Central Government restricts transfers to specified countries or territories, while other applicable laws still apply.
why: The Act authorizes transfer of personal data outside India subject to restrictions the Central Government may specify, and does not override stricter restrictions under other Indian laws.
bad: All transfers outside India are automatically prohibited.
Any overseas provider can receive data with no conditions.
The Act means sector-specific transfer rules no longer matter.

q: A one-time event registration has ended, and no law requires keeping attendees’ dietary preference data. What is the best practice?
a: Erase the data once the purpose is no longer served, while retaining only information required by law.
why: Section 8(7) requires erasure when the specified purpose is no longer served unless retention is necessary for compliance with law. Rule 8 also sets specified erasure periods and requires at least one year of certain processing data and logs for purposes in the Seventh Schedule.
law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 8(7); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 8(1)–(3)
bad: Keep it for future events without telling attendees.
Move it to an archive and consider that deletion.
Share it with sponsors to recover event costs.

q: A service describes consent withdrawal only in a dense terms page and gives no clear path. What should it improve?
a: Make the notice clear and provide a practical communication link or means for withdrawing consent and exercising rights.
why: The Rules require notice in clear and plain language, independently understandable, with links or means to withdraw consent, exercise rights and make complaints.
bad: Leave the flow as-is if the legal team approved the terms.
Make withdrawal harder than sign-up to reduce churn.
Replace the notice with a vague “we value privacy” statement.

q: A company says its processor caused a breach, so the company has no duties. Is that correct?
a: No. The Data Fiduciary remains responsible for compliance for processing carried out on its behalf.
why: Section 8(1) places responsibility on the Data Fiduciary for compliance with the Act in respect of processing undertaken by it or on its behalf, including through a processor.
bad: Yes, a vendor contract transfers every statutory obligation.
Yes, unless the Data Principal has paid for the service.
Yes, if the vendor is located in another country.

q: A user wants a single place to manage, review and withdraw consent given to multiple services. Which statutory concept is designed for this?
a: A registered Consent Manager, acting as a single point of contact through an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform.
why: The Act defines a Consent Manager as a person registered with the Board who acts as a single point of contact to enable a Data Principal to give, manage, review and withdraw consent through an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform.
bad: An unregistered advertising network that trades consent records.
A Data Processor that can change purposes without permission.
A company help desk that silently opts users into marketing.

q: A user submits a correction request using someone else’s identity and false documents. What does the Act expect of Data Principals?
a: They must furnish only authentic information when exercising rights and not impersonate another person.
why: Data Principals have duties under section 15, including furnishing only verifiably authentic information when exercising rights and not impersonating another person.
bad: The company must accept every request without verification.
Users have no duties under the Act.
The company may publish the documents to expose the user.

q: A breach affects users, but the company thinks notice might cause reputational harm. What governs its notification duty?
a: The statutory and prescribed notification requirements—not reputational preference—govern notice to the Board and affected Data Principals.
why: Section 8(6) requires the Data Fiduciary to intimate the Board and each affected Data Principal of a personal data breach in the prescribed manner.
law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 8(6); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 7
bad: Notify only if a user discovers the breach.
Notify only the regulator, never affected people.
Wait until every detail is certain before taking required steps.

q: A ride-share app asks for consent to use trip data for safety alerts and unrelated partner advertising in one checkbox. What is the better approach?
a: Separate the purposes and let the person make a specific, informed choice about each purpose.
why: Consent must be specific and informed, and the notice should clearly describe the purpose. Combining unrelated purposes undermines meaningful choice.
law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 6(1); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 3
bad: Keep one checkbox because both uses involve trip data.
Treat accepting the ride-share terms as consent to all partner use.
Let advertising partners decide whether consent was specific.

q: A support intern can download every customer record, though their work needs only ticket status. What should the privacy lead do?
a: Restrict access to the information necessary for the intern’s role and maintain appropriate safeguards.
why: Reasonable security safeguards are required to protect personal data. Limiting unnecessary access reduces the likelihood and impact of unauthorized disclosure.
bad: Keep broad access because the intern is an employee.
Allow downloads to personal devices for convenience.
Wait until a data breach occurs before adjusting permissions.

q: A platform asks a 16-year-old to confirm their own consent for processing. What additional step does the Act generally require?
a: Obtain verifiable consent of the parent or lawful guardian before processing the child’s personal data, subject to applicable exemptions.
why: A child is an individual under 18, and section 9 generally requires verifiable parental or guardian consent before processing a child’s personal data.
bad: Accept the minor’s confirmation as adult consent.
Ask for parental consent only if the child requests deletion.
Assume every educational purpose is automatically exempt.

q: A company finds a person’s data in a publicly accessible source and wants to reuse it. What should it check?
a: Whether the Act’s scope or a specific exemption applies; public availability alone should not be treated as a blanket permission.
why: The Act excludes certain personal data made or caused to be made publicly available by the Data Principal or under a legal obligation, but the facts and statutory conditions matter.
bad: Assume anything viewable online can be used for any purpose.
Assume the Act always applies identically to every public record.
Sell the data because it was found without a login.

q: A service wants to make rights requests usable for people with disabilities. What should it provide?
a: An accessible means for the Data Principal to exercise rights and make a grievance, with required information about how to do so.
why: The Act provides rights including access, correction, erasure and grievance redressal. The Rules require the notice to describe means to exercise those rights and make complaints.
law: DPDP Act, 2023, ss. 11–13; DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 3(c)
bad: Only accept requests through an inaccessible app flow.
Require a person to publicly disclose sensitive details.
Hide the request method in a lengthy policy document.

q: A company proposes collecting personal data “just in case” a useful purpose appears later. What should the team require first?
a: Identify a lawful, specific purpose and ensure the processing fits a permitted basis before collection.
why: The Act permits processing for a lawful purpose, based on consent or a certain legitimate use. A vague possible future use is not itself a stated purpose.
bad: Collect now and decide on a purpose later.
Treat possession of the data as permission to use it.
Let each department invent a purpose after collection.
